title: Working Through Conflict
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli and Pietaris argue that nearly every conflict goes wrong for the same reasons, whether it is a quarrel over washing-up or a co-founder split, but that the right response changes with the stakes. They sort conflicts into low, medium and high stakes and give each a different working posture, illustrated with short case vignettes (Sam and the mug, Anna and Victor, Daniel and Marie, Priya and her voice notes). Low-stakes friction should be raised early and lightly so it does not accumulate into a disproportionate outburst. Medium-stakes conflict rewards structure, preparation and a clear choice between airing a grievance and solving a problem. High-stakes conflict calls for specialist professionals, careful written communication and attention to self-care. The closing move is the counterintuitive observation that people get worse at conflict just as stakes rise, and that the goal should be a state of affairs both sides can live with rather than a win.
points: Unspoken small irritations pile up so that the eventual reaction is calibrated to the running total, which makes the other person feel ambushed; raise things early and lightly instead.

At medium stakes, choose a deliberate moment, flag the conversation beforehand, and separate the specific incident from the larger pattern so the other person is not asked to defend a year of behaviour at once.
Be honest with yourself about whether you want to air a grievance or solve a problem, because announcing the second while wanting the first leaves you worse off.
At high stakes, hire a specialist rather than a friendly generalist, assume anything you write may be read by a judge, and use friends for support but professionals for advice.
The aim in any conflict is a settlement both people can live with, not a contest with a winner.
quotes: People stop listening because they’re rehearsing their next point. They argue against a position rather than the person actually in front of them, so they end up swinging at a straw man. They confuse their preferences with their principles, which makes any compromise feel like a betrayal.

By the time you do say something, your reaction is calibrated to the running total, while the other person, who has only experienced the latest instance, reasonably thinks you’re being disproportionate.

These conflicts reward more structure. It helps to pick a deliberate moment to talk rather than letting the conversation erupt opportunistically, and to flag it beforehand so the other person isn’t ambushed. That gives them time to think rather than time to defend, and signals that you’re taking the issue seriously enough to plan for.

You generally need professionals, like a family solicitor, a mediator, an employment lawyer or a therapist. The consequences of a misstep at this level are large enough that you want someone whose job is to think clearly while you can’t. People often resist this on cost grounds and end up paying far more for the consequences of going it alone.

So, a useful working rule is to assume any message you send during a high-stakes dispute might end up in front of a judge, an arbitrator or someone else’s lawyer. Most won’t, but writing as if they might removes a whole category of regret.

The counterintuitive thing about stakes is that most people get worse at conflict as the stakes rise, when actually they need to get better. The pull is in the wrong direction at exactly the wrong moment: less sleep, more fear, fewer reliable advisers, a stronger urge to win. All when the cost of winning badly is highest.

The unhelpful instinct in any of these is to treat the conflict as a contest with a winner. Most disagreements between people are problems to be solved together, even when one party has been clearly in the wrong. The aim throughout is a state of affairs both people can live with going forward, with as little damage along the way as possible.
